clinicalPearls: Chronic meningitis is defined by a characteristic neurologic syndrome persisting beyond 4 weeks together with a sustained CSF inflammatory response (white cell count >5/uL); appropriate treatment hinges entirely on identifying the underlying cause.

Five disease categories account for most cases: meningeal infections, malignancy, autoimmune inflammatory disorders, chemical meningitis, and parameningeal infections; some recurrent cases reflect monogenic autoinflammatory disorders.

Cardinal manifestations are persistent nonfocal headache, signs of hydrocephalus, cranial neuropathies, radiculopathies, and cognitive or personality change; classic meningeal signs (Kernig/Brudzinski) are actually uncommon in the chronic form.

Basal meningitis, where exudate collects at the skull base, presents as multiple cranial neuropathies; lower cranial nerves are involved more often because the inflammatory exudate gravitates to the base of the brain.

Spinal involvement produces multiple radiculopathies (radicular pain, sensory loss, weakness, sphincter dysfunction) and may progress to arachnoiditis with clumping of lower nerve roots, again because cells settle at the bottom of the intrathecal space.

Two clinical forms exist: a chronic persistent form and a recurrent form in which all clinical and CSF abnormalities resolve completely between discrete episodes (e.g., Mollaret's meningitis from HSV-2, chemical leak from epidermoid tumor, autoimmune conditions, drug hypersensitivity).

Worldwide, M. tuberculosis is the most common infectious cause, followed by Cryptococcus neoformans; in immunosuppressed patients these may present with little or no headache, fever, or meningeal signs and even a pauci-cellular CSF.

In most chronic (non-recurrent) meningitides mononuclear cells predominate; a neutrophilic CSF after 3 weeks points to Nocardia, Actinomyces, Brucella, certain fungi (Blastomyces, Candida, Histoplasma, Aspergillus, Pseudallescheria, Cladophialophora), or noninfectious causes (SLE, chemical meningitis).

An eosinophilic CSF response suggests parasitic disease (Angiostrongylus, Gnathostoma, Baylisascaris, Toxocara, cysticercosis, schistosomiasis, echinococcosis, toxoplasmosis), coccidioidal fungal meningitis (6-20% eosinophils with lymphocytic pleocytosis), neoplasia, or sarcoidosis.

Meningeal enhancement patterns localize the process: leptomeningeal enhancement follows gyri and basal cisterns (typical of infection), whereas pachymeningeal enhancement is thick, linear or nodular along dura/falx/tentorium (e.g., lymphoma, IgG4-related disease).

In about one-third of cases the cause remains undiagnosed despite thorough evaluation; many causative organisms require weeks of culture, so diagnostic patience is balanced against the risk of progressive neurologic deterioration.

Repeated large-volume lumbar CSF samples (three or more), and if needed cervical cisternal sampling near the basal meninges, raise the yield for fungal and malignant causes; ventricular fluid may appear sterile despite active lower lumbar infection.
harrison.pathophysiology: Chronic inflammation of the meninges (pia, arachnoid, dura) generates neurologic deficits whose pattern is determined by the anatomic site of inflammation and its consequences. CSF, produced by the choroid plexus and circulating from the ventricles through the basal cisterns over the convexities to arachnoid villi, provides a conduit for rapid spread of infectious or infiltrative processes over the brain, cord, and nerve roots; organisms may also track along perivascular (Virchow-Robin) spaces into brain parenchyma. Intracranial inflammation stimulates meningeal nociceptive fibers (headache, neck/back pain) and may obstruct CSF flow at the cerebral aqueduct or arachnoid villi, causing hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure. Inflammatory exudate seeded around the brainstem and cranial nerves at the skull base produces basal meningitis with multiple cranial neuropathies, while spinal exudate injures nerve roots and may encircle the cord to cause myelopathy. Vasculitis of subarachnoid vessels can lead to infarction and cognitive/behavioral decline. A recently identified dural lymphatic system drains the dura, but its role in chronic meningitis is not yet established.
additionalDifferentials: Infectious: M. tuberculosis, Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii, syphilis, Lyme disease (Bannwarth's syndrome), Brucella, Nocardia, Actinomyces, Whipple's disease, partially treated bacterial meningitis, parameningeal infection
Fungal: Coccidioides, Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Candida, Aspergillus, Sporothrix
Parasitic/helminthic: cysticercosis (Taenia solium), Gnathostoma, Angiostrongylus, Baylisascaris, Toxoplasma, trypanosomiasis, Acanthamoeba/Balamuthia
Viral: HSV-2 (Mollaret's, recurrent), mumps, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, enteroviruses (in agammaglobulinemia/B-cell depletion), HIV acute retroviral syndrome
Malignancy: carcinomatous/lymphomatous meningitis (breast, lung, stomach, pancreas, melanoma, leukemia, gliomatosis)
Inflammatory/autoimmune: neurosarcoidosis, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome, Behcet's, SLE, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, IgG4-related hypertrophic pachymeningitis, primary CNS vasculitis, Sjogren's
Monogenic autoinflammatory: TRAPS, CAPS, NOMID, complement factor I deficiency
Chemical: leakage from epidermoid/dermoid tumor, craniopharyngioma, cholesteatoma; drug hypersensitivity (NSAIDs, sulfonamides, IVIG, others)
infectionMimics: Carcinomatous or lymphomatous meningitis (CSF seeding by malignant cells)
Neurosarcoidosis (low CSF glucose can mimic tuberculous/fungal meningitis)
Chemical meningitis from leaking epidermoid/dermoid cyst or craniopharyngioma
Primary CNS or systemic vasculitis with meningitis and stroke
nonInfectiousMimics: Subarachnoid hemorrhage in the preceding week presenting with xanthochromia and pleocytosis
Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome and Behcet's syndrome (recurrent forms)
additionalInvestigations: Measure opening CSF pressure; brain imaging before LP if raised ICP is suspected, as a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus risks herniation
CSF cell count and differential, glucose, protein, Gram's stain; bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures (large volumes)
CSF VDRL (highly specific, low sensitivity); serum treponemal antibodies; consider empiric neurosyphilis treatment if CSF VDRL negative but serum positive with unexplained pleocytosis
Cryptococcal antigen, India ink/fungal wet mount, oligoclonal bands, and cytology/flow cytometry for malignant cells

Pathogen-specific PCR; broad-range 16s rRNA PCR (bacteria, useful in partially treated meningitis), 18s/28s rRNA PCR (fungi), CSF beta-glucan assay, and unbiased metagenomic next-generation sequencing for enigmatic cases
Contrast-enhanced MRI/CT of brain and spinal cord to detect meningeal enhancement, parameningeal infection, cord encasement, or nodular deposits; angiography if arteritis/stroke suspected

Systemic workup: tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay, chest radiograph or chest CT/MRI and sputum exam, urinalysis, CBC, renal/liver function, alkaline phosphatase, ESR, ANA, anti-Ro/anti-La, rheumatoid factor, serum IgG4
FDG-PET to locate a systemic biopsy site in suspected carcinomatous meningitis or sarcoidosis; genetic testing for monogenic autoinflammatory disorders
Meningeal biopsy targeting contrast-enhancing regions when CSF is non-diagnostic and the patient is severely disabled, needs ventricular decompression, or is deteriorating rapidly
redFlags: Signs of raised intracranial pressure (vomiting, drowsiness, papilledema, visual loss, impaired upgaze, sixth-nerve palsy) warranting imaging before lumbar puncture
Rapidly progressive neurologic deterioration requiring urgent treatment rather than awaiting culture results
Multiple progressive cranial neuropathies or evolving radiculopathy/myelopathy indicating widespread CSF dissemination
Focal cerebral signs suggesting brain abscess, parameningeal infection, or infarction
Immunosuppression or untreated HIV, where meningeal signs are attenuated and any persistent headache or mental status change mandates CSF examination
Low CSF glucose with lymphocytic pleocytosis, prompting empiric coverage for tuberculosis given the potential for devastation within weeks
harrison.prognosis: Outcome depends on the underlying etiology and the speed of diagnosis and treatment; many causes are effectively treatable, but untreated disease produces progressive, potentially fatal damage to the CNS, cranial nerves, and roots. Even with treatment, tuberculous meningitis carries high rates of morbidity. Fatal levels of raised intracranial pressure can occur (notably in cryptococcal meningitis) even without ventricular enlargement, and repetitive or continuous CSF drainage may be needed to prevent abrupt deterioration and death. Some recurrent forms (e.g., chronic benign lymphocytic meningitis) resolve over 2-6 months.
pitfalls: Performing lumbar puncture before imaging when raised ICP from a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus exists risks brain herniation
Assuming a normal or pauci-cellular CSF excludes meningitis in immunosuppressed or HIV patients, in whom signs are attenuated
Relying on a single small-volume CSF sample; fungal and malignant causes often require repeated large-volume sampling, and some organisms take weeks to grow in culture
Interpreting a transient response to empiric glucocorticoids as confirmation of a noninfectious cause, since tuberculosis, cysticercosis, and lymphoma may also respond temporarily
Overlooking false-negative cryptococcal antigen or CSF VDRL results due to the prozone effect at high antibody/antigen titers
Attributing dural enhancement to disease when it can be a benign post-LP, post-neurosurgical, post-concussion, or post-CSF-leak finding
Failing to recognize that ventricular CSF can appear sterile while active infection persists in the lower lumbar space
harrison.severityClassification: No formal grading scale is given; severity is gauged clinically by the rate of neurologic progression, the presence of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus, and the degree of disability, which together determine whether to await culture results or proceed to meningeal biopsy and empiric therapy.
